content: The text provided appears to be a detailed list of references and systematic reviews related to various studies on physical activity, health outcomes, media use, and behavioral issues among children, adolescents, and adults. 1. A study conducted in the Community of Madrid examined adolescents' health and behaviors, as published in Aten Primaria in 2010 (Volume 42, Issue 2, Pages 79-85). 2. Shashi Kumar R and colleagues investigated the interplay between media exposure, sexual activity, and academic performance in adolescents. Their findings were published in the Armed Forces Medical Journal of India in 2013 (Volume 69, Issue 2, Pages 138-143). 3. Vassiloudis I and collaborators explored the relationship between adherence to the Mediterranean diet, energy balance behaviors, and academic performance in Greek primary school children. This study was published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior in 2014 (Volume 46, Issue 3, Pages 164-170). 4. O'Dea JA and Mugridge AC demonstrated that the nutritional quality of breakfast and physical activity independently predict literacy and numeracy scores in children, even after adjusting for socioeconomic status. Their research appeared in Health Education Research in 2012 (Volume 27, Issue 6, Pages 975-985). 5. Hoza B and colleagues conducted a randomized trial to assess the effects of aerobic physical activity on symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in young children. The results were published in the Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology in 2014. 6. Howie EK, Beets MW, and Pate RR found that acute classroom exercise breaks improve on-task behavior in 4th and 5th-grade students, with a dose-response relationship. Their findings were published in Mental Health and Physical Activity in 2014 (Volume 7, Issue 2, Pages 65-71). 7. Gentile DA and colleagues provided evidence of bidirectional causality between video game playing, attention problems, and impulsiveness. This study was published in Psychology of Popular Media Culture in 2012 (Volume 1, Issue 1, Pages 62-70). 8. Hoffert SL examined the impact of home media use on children's academic achievement and behavior, with findings published in Child Development in 2010 (Volume 81, Issue 5, Pages 1598-1619). 9. Janssen I, Boyce WF, and Pickett W investigated the association between screen time and physical violence among Canadian youth aged 10 to 16 years. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Public Health in 2012 (Volume 57, Issue 2, Pages 325-331). 10. Lemmens JS, Valkenburg PM, and Peter J studied the effects of pathological gaming on aggressive behavior, with results published in the Journal of Youth and Adolescence in 2011 (Volume 40, Issue 1, Pages 38-47). 11. Parkes A and colleagues conducted longitudinal research using the UK Millennium Cohort Study to determine whether television and electronic games predict children's psychosocial adjustment. Their findings were published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2013 (Volume 98, Issue 5, Pages 341-348). 12. Robertson LA, McAnally HM, and Hancox RJ explored the relationship between childhood and adolescent television viewing and antisocial behavior in early adulthood. This study was published in Pediatrics in 2013 (Volume 131, Issue 3, Pages 439-446). 13. Swing EL, Gentile DA, Anderson CA, and Walsh DA examined the impact of television and video game exposure on the development of attention problems. Their research appeared in Pediatrics in 2010 (Volume 126, Issue 2, Pages 214-221). 14. Willoughby T, Adachi PJ, and Good M conducted a longitudinal study on the association between violent video game play and aggression among adolescents. The findings were published in Developmental Psychology in 2012 (Volume 48, Issue 4, Pages 1044-1057). 15. Demirok M and colleagues investigated the relationship between computer games and reported anger in young individuals. Their study was published in the Australian Journal of Guidance and Counselling in 2012 (Volume 22, Issue 1, Pages 33-43). 16. Griffiths LJ and collaborators examined the associations between sport and screen entertainment with mental health problems in 5-year-old children. This study was published in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2010 (Volume 7, Article 30). 17. Przybylski AK studied the relationship between electronic gaming and psychosocial adjustment, with findings published in Pediatrics in 2014 (Volume 134, Issue 3, Pages e716-e722). 18. Rech RR, Halpern R, Tedesco A, and Santos DF analyzed the prevalence and characteristics of bullying victims and perpetrators. Their research appeared in the Journal of Pediatrics in 2013 (Volume 89, Issue 2, Pages 164-170). 19. Rosen L demonstrated that media and technology use predict ill-being among children, preteens, and teenagers, independent of the negative health impacts of exercise and eating habits. This study was published in Computers in Human Behavior in 2014 (Volume 35, Pages 364-375). 20. Shokouhi-Moqhaddam S and colleagues explored the correlation between computer games and adolescent behavioral problems. Their findings were published in Addict Health in 2013 (Volume 5, Issues 1-2, Pages 43-50). 21. Singh GK and Yu SM examined the impact of ethnic-immigrant status and obesity-related risk factors on behavioral problems among U.S. children and adolescents. This study was published in Scientifica in 2012 (Article ID 648152). 22. Van Egmond-Frohlich AW, Weghuber D, and de ZM investigated the association of ADHD symptoms with physical activity, media time, and food intake in children and adolescents. Their research appeared in PLoS One in 2012 (Volume 7, Issue 11, Article e49781). 23. A systematic review of evidence on physical activity for adults aged 18 to under 65 years was conducted to assess its association with health-related outcomes, including dose-response relationships and variations by type or domain of physical activity. The review identified 75 studies published between 2017 and 2019, with 35 excluded due to design, population, or quality concerns. Only two systematic reviews were rated as having high credibility, while others ranged from moderate to critically low credibility. 24. The AMSTAR 2 tool was used to critically appraise systematic reviews, with ratings based on factors such as study design, literature search strategy, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. Most reviews had limitations in design, execution, and reporting, with only a few achieving high credibility.
